premises.text: Competitive programming sites focus on a limited set of textbook algorithms rather than real-world problems.
premises.evidence_span: sites like ACM and Topcoder focus on a small set of textbook algorithms, whereas in the real world, you work on things ranging from machine learning to artificial intelligence to distributed systems to build real products.

premises.text: HackerRank provides a competitive league for hackers to solve real-world problems.
premises.evidence_span: we are building the competitive league for hackers to solve real world problems.

premises.text: Challenges on HackerRank are classified into levels of difficulty based on user performance.
premises.evidence_span: the difficulty level of a challenge is determined by the number of users who solve it, which means the ranking is completely dynamic.

premises.text: Companies can provide real datasets for challenges to enhance the competitive experience.
premises.evidence_span: we are inviting companies to give us real data sets or problems that they're actually working on.

premises.text: HackerRank allows users to code and test their solutions in various programming languages.
premises.evidence_span: you can compile and test, ideally you should get the output immediately, but maybe there are some network issues or my code is really bad.

premises.text: HackerRank archives challenges and code snippets to help users learn from each other.
premises.evidence_span: we decided to put up, archive the challenges every two weeks and release all the code snippets so that hackers can learn from others to write optimal algorithms.

premises.text: HackerRank aims to centralize the world's most interesting programming problems.
premises.evidence_span: we are building the largest collection of the world's most interesting problems for hackers to solve.

value.text: Hackers can engage in competitive programming and solve real-world problems.
